What California's altered-image rule actually requires

Updated 25 August 2026 · 6 min

If you shoot listings in California, a rule changed underneath you on 1 January 2026. Most of the coverage since has been either alarming or vague, and the two failure modes it produces are equally expensive: agents who stop doing normal photo editing they were always allowed to do, and agents who carry on with AI imagery and have no idea they now owe a disclosure.

Here is the shape of it, as plainly as we can put it.

The rule

AB 723, approved 10 October 2025, added §10140.8 to the California Business and Professions Code. It applies to a broker, a salesperson, or a person acting on their behalf — which is worth pausing on, because that last clause reaches your photographer, your marketing agency and your video vendor, not just you.

Where an advertisement or promotional material for the sale of real property includes a digitally altered image, it must:

  • carry a conspicuous statement that the image has been modified, and
  • provide a link to the original, unaltered image by website, URL, or QR code

Where the advertisement is on a website, the unaltered image itself has to be there.

Two duties, not one. This is the part most summaries get wrong: a disclaimer on its own does not satisfy the statute. A sentence saying "some images have been digitally enhanced" meets the first requirement and simply ignores the second.

What is explicitly not covered

This is the part worth reading twice, because it is where most of the anxiety lives and none of it belongs:

lighting · sharpening · white balance · colour correction · angle · straightening · cropping · exposure

None of these make an image "digitally altered" for the purposes of the statute. The reasoning is coherent: they do not change the representation of the property. A brightened kitchen is the same kitchen.

So the ordinary work every listing photographer has always done is untouched. If your editing does not change what is actually there, you are outside the rule.

What is covered

The line the statute draws is about representation, not about tooling. If an image shows a buyer something that was not there — or hides something that was — it is altered, whether the change came from Photoshop, an AI model, or a very patient intern.

In practice that means virtual staging, sky replacement, removing a neighbour's car, adding a fire to a fireplace, and generated imagery of any kind.

The national rule that was already there

AB 723 is a California statute, and the reaction to it has slightly obscured the fact that NAR's Code of Ethics already required this nationally. Article 12 requires REALTORS® to present a true picture in advertising, and Standard of Practice 12-5 requires disclosing the status of any altered photograph. That binds every REALTOR® in every state, independent of any MLS rule or state statute.

If you are outside California, you are not outside the duty. You are outside the part that specifies how — the link to the original.

What it costs to get wrong

MLS boards commonly fine non-disclosure of virtual staging in the $500–$5,000 range, varying by board. The statutory exposure is a separate question and one for your broker's counsel.

The larger cost is not the fine. A disclosure failure surfaces when a buyer feels misled, which is exactly when it is most expensive to be the agent who listed it.

Where AI video sits

A video built from photographs of a real property is a generated image under any sensible reading, and it does carry the duty.

That is not an argument against using it. It is an argument for treating the disclosure as part of the deliverable rather than something bolted on afterwards. If your vendor hands you a file and a suggested caption, you have half of what the statute asks for and all of the liability.

The workable version is: an on-screen mark, and a page carrying the original photographs, reachable by URL or QR. That page is the artefact §10140.8 asks you to link to. It is not a courtesy and there is no substitute for it.

One thing worth checking with your vendor

Ask whether they edit your photographs.

It sounds like a quality question and it is not — it is the one that determines whether the originals page you are relying on actually contains originals. A vendor who colour-corrects your stills before generating from them has given you a page of their images, and the link you are publishing no longer points at the unaltered source.

The short version

  1. Normal photo editing is fine and always was. Do not stop.
  2. If an image changes what is actually there, you owe two things: a conspicuous statement, and a link to the original.
  3. A disclaimer alone does not satisfy the rule.
  4. NAR Article 12 means the duty to disclose exists nationally regardless.
  5. The rule reaches people acting on your behalf, so it is your vendor's problem too — but it stays your name on the listing.

This is not legal advice, and the summaries above are drawn from secondary reporting of the statute rather than from a legal opinion. Read the AB 723 bill text directly, and have your broker's counsel review your disclosure language before you rely on it. Rules also vary by MLS and by state.
